questions.why: Every cell, prokaryotic or eukaryotic, is enclosed by a cell membrane that separates its interior from the surroundings.
questions.deep: Nuclei and mitochondria exist only in eukaryotes, and animal cells have no cell wall, so none of those features is universal. The phospholipid bilayer boundary is the one structure all cells share. Think: every cell has a 'skin.'

questions.why: Phospholipids self-assemble into the bilayer that forms the basic fabric of every cell membrane.
questions.deep: Their water-loving heads face the watery environments on both sides while their water-fearing tails hide inside the sheet. Proteins and cholesterol are embedded in this sheet, but the continuous double layer itself is phospholipid. Triglycerides store energy, cellulose builds plant walls, and glycogen stores glucose.

variants.stem: The channels and carriers that move specific ions across the cell membrane are made of which type of molecule?
Transport 'holes' that let certain molecules pass into and out of the cell belong to which macromolecule class?

Which class of biological molecule forms the passageways that shuttle ions across a membrane?
Complete the statement: membrane channels that admit specific molecules are made of ___.

questions.why: Membrane channels and carriers are proteins that span the bilayer and let specific ions and molecules pass.
questions.deep: The lipid core of the membrane repels charged particles like Na⁺ and K⁺, so they need protein doorways. Channels form selective tunnels, while carriers change shape to ferry cargo. This is the basis of facilitated diffusion and active transport.

A student labels a cell diagram. What name belongs to the material occupying the space between the membrane and the nucleus?

What is the cell filled with?

Which substance makes up the bulk of a cell's interior?

questions.why: Cytoplasm is the gel-like material filling the cell interior between the membrane and the nucleus.
questions.deep: Cytoplasm includes the cytosol plus all suspended organelles. Nucleoplasm is the fluid inside the nucleus, blood plasma is the liquid part of blood, and interstitial fluid surrounds cells from outside.

questions.why: An organelle is a specialized structure inside a cell that carries out a specific function, like a tiny organ.
questions.deep: The name literally means 'little organ.' Some organelles are membrane-bound, such as mitochondria and lysosomes, while others, like ribosomes, are not. A group of similar cells is a tissue, not an organelle.

Check every item that a newly formed cell of any species contains.
Select all that apply: structures or molecules that cells of every organism possess.
Which components would you expect inside every newly made cell? Select all that apply.

questions.why: All cells carry DNA as their instructions, RNA as working copies, and ribosomes to build proteins from those messages.
questions.deep: A nucleus is absent from bacteria, and chloroplasts occur only in plants and algae, so neither is universal. Even the simplest bacterium runs the DNA → RNA → protein workflow. A few specialized cells, such as mature human red blood cells, eject their DNA later, which is why the stems specify newly formed cells.

variants.stem: Select all that apply: which parts does every cell consist of?

Select all that apply: features present in even the simplest cell.
Which of these would you find in a cell of any organism? Select all that apply.
Select all that apply: parts that no cell lacks.

questions.why: The minimal kit shared by every cell is a cell membrane boundary, cytoplasm interior, and nucleic acids carrying genetic information.
questions.deep: Cell walls are missing from animal cells, and mitochondria are missing from prokaryotes. Bacteria handle energy release using their membrane and cytoplasm instead of mitochondria. Membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleic acids appear in every newly formed cell.

A biology instructor asks how cells originate. Which answer covers the two broad routes?

Which pair names the two ways living things produce new cells?
Complete the statement: a cell's life begins with ___.

questions.why: Cell theory states that new cells arise only from existing cells through sexual or asexual reproduction.
questions.deep: Asexual reproduction, such as binary fission or mitotic division, produces genetically identical cells, while sexual reproduction combines gametes. Pasteur's experiments disproved spontaneous generation. The other option pairs are metabolic or molecular processes, not routes to new cells.

questions.why: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together on a shared function.
questions.deep: The body's hierarchy runs cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism. The four primary tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous. Similar cells teaming up is the defining feature of the tissue level.

questions.why: An organ combines two or more tissue types that cooperate to perform a specific function.
questions.deep: The stomach, for example, contains epithelial tissue for secretion, muscle tissue for churning, connective tissue for support, and nervous tissue for control. Similar cells alone make only a tissue, and several organs together make a system.

questions.why: Ribosomes are the granules where amino acids are joined into proteins, so every marked dot is a correct tap.
questions.deep: In the diagram the small bright dots are ribosomes: some stud the folded ER membranes and one floats free in the cytosol. The large purple sphere is the nucleus, the orange oval is a mitochondrion, and the green stack is the Golgi. Bound ribosomes mainly build proteins for export, while free ones build proteins used inside the cell.

questions.deep: The rough ER folds and processes the proteins its ribosomes make. Smooth ER has no ribosomes and handles lipid synthesis and detoxification. The Golgi and lysosomes never carry attached ribosomes.

questions.why: The Golgi complex modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles for delivery to their destinations.
questions.deep: Think of it as the cell's post office: cargo arrives from the ER, gets finished and labeled, then ships out. It does not build proteins from scratch — ribosomes do that. ATP production belongs to mitochondria, DNA storage to the nucleus, and organelle digestion to lysosomes.

questions.why: The Golgi sits in the cytoplasm close to the nucleus, positioned to receive vesicles from the nearby ER.
questions.deep: The ER is continuous with the nuclear envelope, so a perinuclear Golgi keeps the ER → Golgi → membrane shipping line short. The Golgi is never inside the nucleus or mitochondria, and it is not embedded in the plasma membrane.

questions.why: Vacuoles are membrane-bound sacs used for storage, digestion of materials, and isolation or removal of wastes.
questions.deep: In plants the central vacuole stores water and maintains turgor pressure. Food vacuoles partner with lysosomes to digest material, and some protists use contractile vacuoles to pump out excess water. Protein assembly belongs to ribosomes and ATP production to mitochondria.

questions.why: A typical mature plant cell consolidates its storage into a single large central vacuole.
questions.deep: That one vacuole can occupy most of the cell's volume, pressing the cytoplasm into a thin layer against the wall. Its water pressure (turgor) keeps leaves and stems firm. Young, dividing plant cells may start with several small vacuoles that later merge into one.

questions.deep: Animal vacuoles are typically small and often temporary, used for storage or transport. Plant cells invest in one large central vacuole for water balance and support. 'No vacuoles in animal cells' is a common misconception.

questions.deep: Vesicles bud from one membrane and fuse with another, keeping their contents separated from the cytosol. Lysosomes can be viewed as specialized digestive vesicles. A protein pore, a nucleus, and an external coat are all different structures.

questions.deep: The cytoskeleton also includes thinner actin microfilaments and intermediate filaments. Microtubules double as transport tracks and form the mitotic spindle, cilia, and flagella. They are built from the protein tubulin.

questions.why: Microtubules act as internal struts that support the cell and organize its interior.
questions.deep: Motor proteins walk along microtubules carrying vesicles, and the spindle that separates chromosomes is made of them. Digestion is handled by lysosomes, genetic instructions by DNA, and lipid synthesis by smooth ER.

questions.deep: Pairs of α- and β-tubulin stack into long hollow tubes. Microtubules are not made of carbohydrate, lipid, or nucleic acid. Because the spindle is protein-based, drugs that block tubulin assembly stop cell division.

questions.deep: Cytoplasm equals cytosol plus organelles, so the two terms are related but not identical. Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol. Nuclear fluid is nucleoplasm, fluid between cells is interstitial fluid, and blood's liquid is plasma.

Complete the statement: cytosol consists primarily of ___.

questions.why: Cytosol is mostly water, with ions, sugars, amino acids, and proteins dissolved or suspended in it.
questions.deep: Water makes up roughly 70 percent or more of cytosol and acts as the cell's solvent. Proteins are the largest dissolved fraction, but water still dominates by far. This is why dehydration quickly disrupts cellular chemistry.
